newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Uganda offers hope in Africa's AIDS battle.
newsitem.headline: Uganda offers hope in Africa's AIDS battle.

text.p: Uganda, an early casualty of the AIDS epidemic, is winning the battle against the killer disease in urban areas, offering hope to the rest of Africa, Prime Minister Abednego Kintu-Musoke said on Wednesday.

In the past few years the rate of infection has dropped from 30 to 15 percent of the population in some towns, testament to a public health policy which refuses to sweep the problem under the carpet, he told a World Economic Forum conference in Harare.
"Our policy in fighting AIDS has been to give it a face and expose it as a deadly enemy of the population," Kintu-Musoke said.
"As a result of the openness we have been able to achieve a very high degree of HIV awareness which has lead to behaviour changes leading to the decline in the rate of infection."

The health problem remains acute in Uganda, with 1.5 million out of a population of 20 million infected with the HIV virus which causes AIDS and over 50 percent of the health facilities taken up by AIDS patients.
Uganda also has more than a million AIDS orphans.

But the country's experience of confronting the problem head-on in order to change sexual behaviour could be used to help other countries on the continent hardest-hit by AIDS (Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome), he said.
"The HIV/AIDS epidemic is still a serious problem in our region and is likely to remain so for a long time to come. We therefore need the continued commitment of governments."

At the end of 1996 a total of 14 million people were living with HIV infection or AIDS in sub-Saharan Africa, representing 63 percent of ther world's total, according to UNAIDS, the United Nations coordinating body for the disease.

And while the epidemic may be plateauing out in Uganda it is still spreading at alarming rates in many countries, cutting a swathe through the most economically-active section of the population aged between 20 and 45 years.
More than 18 percent of adults in Botswana are infected; 17 percent in Zambia and Zimbabwe.

South Africa, protected in part by the isolation of the aparthied era, has lagged the rest of the continent in the spread of the virus. But latest figures show a worrying increase even there with infection rates now up to six percent.
Former Zaire is another country to have experienced relatively low prevalencee with HIV infection in Kinshasa hovering around five percent.
But following the upheaval of the civil war experts fear the situation in Africa's third largest country could now change, with unpredictable and serious consequences.
